newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK closes Vietnamese camp,moves closer to end saga.
newsitem.headline: HK closes Vietnamese camp,moves closer to end saga.

text.p: Hong Kong closed another chapter of the Vietnamese boatpeople saga on Monday when it shut down a major refugee detention centre before China takes over.
But the Hong Kong government, despite efforts, has clearly failed to meet Beijing's demand to clear all Vietnamese boatpeople from the territory before the sovereignty change.
Over 3,000 remain as the British colony reverts to Beijing's control at midnight on June 30.
The plight of the boat people is a legacy of the Vietnam War when the communist takeover in 1975 forced thousands to make a perilous exodus across the South China Sea.
The survivors who landed here faced a traumatic time, detained behind barbed wire. Some got sanctuary in the West but most were forced back to Vietnam in distressing scenes.
China has repeatedly told Britain all Vietnamese detention camps would have to be emptied out by the handover, but it has not spelled out what will happen to any left behind.

Hong Kong government refugee coordinator Sally Wong said before closing the Whitehead Detention Centre in the rural New Territories, that 3,000 or so asylum-seekers would remain in the territory after the handover.
"We have no plan to take in those who have failed to qualify as refugees" Wong told reporters.

The Whitehead centre, which is now littered with trash, was battered last year when more than 100 detainees staged a massive breakout and torched more than a dozen buildings along their escape. They were all later recaptured.

Currently, the number of boatpeople in Hong Kong is more than 3,800. About 1,600 are deemed refugees waiting for asylum in third countries, 1,850 are regarded as illegal migrants awaiting repatriation, and 270 await screening for their status.
Earlier, a United Nations official in Hong Kong reported some fresh progress in efforts to clear Vietnamese refugees out of the territory before July 1.
Jean-Noel Wetterwald, head of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees in Hong Kong, said fewer-than-expected Vietnamese would be stranded in Hong Kong.
"We are very close to ending the saga of the boat people in Hong Kong," he said. "More than 99 percent of the cases have been solved."

A dozen municipal councillors from the Whitehead area marked the closure of the camp by uncorking a bottle of champagne at the gate when it was locked up. The remaining 270 detainees there were transfered to High Island, the last such camp now in Hong Kong.
Wong also said the government would discuss with the Vietnamese government in the next few weeks ways to speed up the repatriation of the illegal migrants.
"We hope the process can be shortened," she said.
The boatpeople are among the last of a tide of people who fled Vietnam on flimsy boats to Southeast Asian territories after the Communists won the Vietnam War in 1975.
